root.note: al- ‘the’ + zayt ‘olive oil’. Before z the article sounds like az-. The Arabic word itself is traced to Aramaic zayta.

history: Spain is the land of olive oil, and its word for oil is Arabic. Speakers of Andalusian Arabic said az-zayt, ‘the oil’, and Spanish took the whole phrase, article included, as one word: Old Spanish azeyte, modern aceite. The Arabic word meant the juice of the olive, and it is related to Hebrew záyit, ‘olive’. Why did Spanish give up Latin oleum? One suggestion is that its regular Spanish form would have been ojo, exactly the word for ‘eye’. That idea is attractive but cannot be proved. The Latin word survives only in learned óleo, which you meet mostly in painting.
historyEinfach: Aceite is an Arabic word. In al-Andalus, people said az-zayt, ‘the oil’. The word az-zayt has the Arabic word for ‘the’ in it. Spanish took the whole thing as one word. So aceite really means ‘the oil’. The Latin word for oil lives on in Spanish only in óleo, a word used for paintings.

elsewhere.text: If you speak Arabic, you can hear your own word in aceite: the article az- is still there at the start.
Hebrew záyit means the olive itself, and oil is shemen. Arabic and Hebrew share the olive word.
